explanations.explanation: Allies is right. Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah and the other three kings came to the Valley of Siddim as allies, which puts all five on one side. They're on the same team against the four kings. Five kings agreeing on one plan, and I can't get two ovens to agree on one temperature.

Not captives, friend. The text says the latter five came as allies to the Valley of Siddim, so they were on the same side. Captives show up later in the chapter, when the four kings carry off Abram's nephew Lot (Gen 14:12).
Close, but these five weren't rivals to each other. The text says the latter five came as allies. They were all lined up on the same side, against the four kings.

Rebelled it is. For twelve years Sodom's side was subject to Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. Then in the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him went out (Gen 14:5). That's quite a way to end twelve years of going along with it.
Submitting was the twelve-year habit. The text says they had been subject to Chedorlaomer for twelve years, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled. So the habit ended right there.
Retreating comes up later, in the battle itself. In the thirteenth year the text says they rebelled against Chedorlaomer, king of Elam. Rebelling is the move that starts the fight.

The five kings didn't win this one. The text says that as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some men fell into the tar pits, and the survivors fled to the hill country. Then the four kings seized the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah. Five kings went in, and the four kings came out with the loot.

False is right. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and some of their men fell into the tar pits. The survivors ran to the hill country. Then the four kings seized all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah.

Tar pits. The Valley of Siddim was full of them, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some men fell into the pits. The survivors fled to the hill country. I think this part of the story hurts, so I'll just say it plainly and leave it there.
No cave in this text, friend. It says some men fell into the tar pits as they fled. The survivors went to the hill country.

explanations.answer: They get lost in the desert
explanations.explanation: Nothing about a desert here. The Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits, and some of the men fell into them while fleeing. The ones who made it got away to the hill country.

Lot, Abram's nephew. The four kings carried him off along with his possessions, since Lot was living in Sodom. Once Abram heard that his relative had been captured, he mobilized his men (Gen 14:14). So this part of the story turns on family.
Eliezer isn't named anywhere in this story. The text says the four kings carried off Abram's nephew Lot and his possessions. Lot was living in Sodom, and that's how he got caught up in it.
Nahor isn't named in this story either. The man carried off was Abram's nephew Lot, with his possessions. The text says he was living in Sodom.

explanations.answer: He sets out after the four kings
explanations.explanation: He goes after them. Abram mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household, and they set out in pursuit as far as Dan. He heard his relative was captured and he moved. No committee meeting.

explanations.answer: He guards his tents at Mamre
explanations.explanation: Staying home isn't what the text says. Abram mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household, and they set out in pursuit as far as Dan. Those men were trained, and they were sent after the four kings.

explanations.answer: He sends them with a ransom
explanations.explanation: No ransom here, friend. The text says the men set out in pursuit as far as Dan. Abram sent them after the four kings, not to the bargaining table.

explanations.answer: He divides his forces at night
explanations.explanation: That's the one. During the night, Abram divided his forces and routed Chedorlaomer's army. Then he pursued them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus. He had 318 trained men, and I get nervous just dividing a batch of dough in broad daylight.
Not at noon. The text says that during the night, Abram divided his forces and routed Chedorlaomer's army. So the attack came in the dark, in more than one group.

explanations.answer: He calls the five kings for help
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a call to the five kings. It says Abram divided his forces during the night and routed Chedorlaomer's army. That's the plan the text gives us.

True. Abram retrieved all the goods, as well as his relative Lot and his possessions, together with the women and the rest of the people. So the goods came back with the people. That's a big result for 318 men.

The text says the opposite. Abram retrieved all the goods, as well as his relative Lot and his possessions. He also brought back the women and the rest of the people. So the goods did come back, and the right answer is True.
Bread and wine. Melchizedek brought them out to Abram, and the text says he was priest of God Most High. Abram had just come back from a long chase, so I'd say that's a table worth sitting at.
Not figs and raisins. The text says Melchizedek brought out bread and wine. Raisins are welcome at my bakery, but they didn't make this guest list.

Milk and honey isn't in this scene. The text says Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine, since he was priest of God Most High. That's the table this passage sets. I'll save the milk and honey for another day.
True. Melchizedek is king of Salem, and the text says he was priest of God Most High. Two jobs, one man. Meanwhile, I'm still working on keeping one hat straight.
The text says otherwise. Melchizedek is king of Salem, and it adds that he was priest of God Most High. So he held both roles.

explanations.answer: Delivering Abram's enemies into his hand
explanations.explanation: That's it. Melchizedek says, "…blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand." He's speaking of the rescue Abram had just done. Melchizedek puts the praise on God Most High.

explanations.answer: Giving Abram a son in his old age
explanations.explanation: A son isn't what Melchizedek blesses God for here. He says, "…blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand." His blessing is about the victory Abram just had.

explanations.answer: Giving Abram the whole land of Canaan
explanations.explanation: Melchizedek doesn't mention land in his blessing. He says, "…blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand." The blessing is about the enemies Abram had just beaten.

Melchizedek, king of Salem. After he blessed Abram, Abram gave him a tenth of everything. This came after Abram returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him (Gen 14:17). A tenth of everything, and I get dramatic about the last cookie in the box.
Not Bera, king of Sodom. The text says Abram gave a tenth of everything to Melchizedek, right after Melchizedek's blessing. The king of Sodom gets his own moment in the next verse.

Not Mamre. Mamre the Amorite was bound by treaty to Abram, along with his brothers Eshcol and Aner (Gen 14:13). But the text says Abram gave the tenth to Melchizedek, after the blessing. Mamre does come back at the very end of the story, in Abram's last words to the king of Sodom.
Goods. The king of Sodom says, "Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself." On paper, it's a generous offer. Hold onto it, because Abram has something to say about it.
Land isn't in the offer. The king of Sodom says, "Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself." The goods are what he puts on the table for Abram.
There's no city in this offer. The king of Sodom says, "Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself." The goods are the part Abram could keep.

Close, baker, but this one is False. Abram turns the offer down. The king of Sodom says, "Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself." Abram answers that he has raised his hand to the LORD God Most High, and he won't take even a thread or a strap of a sandal (Gen 14:21-23). He's walking away from a whole pile of goods. I think that takes a steady heart. I can't even walk past a free sample without a little taste.

False is right, baker! The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, but Abram says no. He tells the king he has raised his hand to the LORD God Most High, and he won't accept even a thread or a strap of a sandal. He doesn't want the king saying, 'I have made Abram rich' (Gen 14:21-23). So he refuses the whole pile, down to a shoelace-sized scrap. I once got nervous turning down a cracked cookie, and this man turned down a king.

explanations.answer: So the king can't say he made Abram rich
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Abram gives. He says he won't accept anything, "…lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’" He wants the king to have nothing to say about that. Not one thread.

explanations.answer: So the people of Sodom will trust him
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason. Abram says he won't accept anything, "…lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’" It says nothing about the people of Sodom trusting him.

explanations.answer: So the four kings won't come back for it
explanations.explanation: That isn't the reason Abram gives. He says he won't accept anything, "…lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’" The four kings aren't part of his answer.

True, baker! Abram tells the king he will accept nothing except what his men have eaten and the share for the men who went with him. Then he names Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, and says they may take their portion (Gen 14:24). He doesn't force their hand either way. He only says that the share is theirs to take, and the text doesn't say what they did.

Not quite, friend. Abram says he will accept nothing except what his men have eaten and the share for the men who went with him. Then he says of Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, "They may take their portion." (Gen 14:24). So the verse says what the card says, and True is the right answer. Abram keeps nothing for himself, but he doesn't speak for their shares.
